slides.text:
A slice is a flexible list of values of one type. Unlike an array, its length is not written in the type, so it is the list you will use most in Go.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

In this module you will create slices, cut pieces out of them and see what a piece shares, walk them with `range`, and pass them to functions. Grids, nil slices and the traps of cutting come in the next modules, and growing a slice after them.

A slice does not hold values itself. It looks at a stretch of values stored somewhere else, like a window on a wall of boxes. Making a new slice from it opens a new window on the same boxes.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
boxes = 10, 20, 30, 40
window = boxes from 1 to 3
window shows 20, 30

slides.text: Cutting a slice uses two positions with a colon. The first is where the piece starts, and the second is where it stops, and that one is **not** included. Leaving one out means the start or the end.

exercises.title: Write a slice
exercises.guide: Make a slice with its values and read it.

chunks.guide: A slice literal looks like an array literal, but the brackets are empty: no length.

notes.text: Empty brackets: the length is not fixed.

chunks.guide: Indexes and `len` work as they did on arrays.
A position can be replaced the same way.

exercises.title: Empty and made slices
exercises.guide: Declare a slice with no values, then make one with room for values.

chunks.guide: A slice declared without values is `nil`. It has length 0 and can be compared with `nil`.

notes.text: True while the slice has never been given a list.

chunks.guide: `make` builds a slice of a given length. Every position starts at the zero value.

notes.text: Creates the slice with 3 zeroed positions.

chunks.text:
scores := make([]int, 3)
    scores[1] = 8
    fmt.Println(scores, scores == nil)

exercises.title: Make a slice
exercises.guide: Build a slice of 4 ints, set the first one, then print its length and its values.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    ages := ___([]int, 4)
    ages[0] = 30
    fmt.Println(___(ages), ages)
}

exercises.title: Cut a slice
exercises.guide: Take pieces out of a slice with a colon.

chunks.guide: Five letters to cut from.
`[1:3]` starts at index 1 and stops before index 3, so it holds two values.

notes.text: Index 3 is where it stops, and it is left out.

chunks.guide: Leave out the start to begin at 0, or the end to go to the last value.

exercises.title: Share the values
exercises.guide: Change a piece of a slice and look at the original.

chunks.guide: A piece is a new slice that looks at the same values, not a copy of them.

notes.text: A window on nums, with no new values.

chunks.guide: Changing a value through `part` changes it for `nums` too.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `t` starts at index 1 of `s`, so `t[1]` is index 2 of `s`. Both see the change, and `t` holds 20 and 0.

slides.text:
`range` walks a slice and gives two things on every turn: the index and the value. The value is a **copy** of what sits there, so changing it does not change the slice. To change the slice, use the index.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
for each index and value of list
    value is a copy
    list at index is the real one

slides.text: A slice has no copy of its values when you loop: it still looks at the same boxes. If the loop changes a position that is still ahead, the loop will see the new value.

exercises.title: Walk a slice
exercises.guide: Loop over a slice with its index and value.

chunks.guide: Three scores to work with.
`range` gives the index and the value of every position.
`len` is the count of values, so it gives the average.

exercises.title: The value is a copy
exercises.guide: Change values in a loop, with and without the index.

chunks.guide: The value `n` is a copy. Changing it leaves the slice alone.
Use the index to reach the real value in the slice.

exercises.title: Double in place
exercises.guide: Double every price inside the slice, and print the slice.

exercises.title: Same loop, now a slice
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: A slice shares its values with the loop, so `v` at index 2 is already 10: 1 + 2 + 10 is 13. A ranged array would be copied first.

exercises.title: Find the largest
exercises.guide: Find the position of the biggest value.

chunks.guide: `best` holds the index of the biggest value seen so far.
Compare each value with the best one, and keep its index.
The index also gives the value.

exercises.title: Reverse in place
exercises.guide: Reverse a slice by swapping its ends.

chunks.guide: Five values to turn around.
Swap the first with the last, the second with the one before it, and stop halfway.

notes.text: Past the middle, the swaps would undo themselves.

slides.text:
A function receives its own copy of the slice, but that copy looks at the same values as the caller's. So changing a value inside shows outside.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
caller list -> boxes 1, 2, 3
function gets a window on those boxes
function sets box 0 -> caller sees it

slides.text: What the function cannot do is move the caller's window. Giving its parameter a whole new slice only changes the function's own copy.

exercises.title: Change it from a function
exercises.guide: Pass a slice to a function that changes it.

chunks.guide: Unlike an array, a slice shares its values with the caller.
The change shows in the caller.

exercises.title: Zero the last value
exercises.guide: Zero the last value inside a function, then print the slice in main.

exercises.title: A new slice inside
exercises.guide: See what a function can and cannot change.

chunks.guide: Setting a value changes the caller's slice.
A new slice only moves this function's own copy. The caller keeps its slice.

notes.text: The caller never sees this assignment.

chunks.guide: The caller's slice kept only the first change.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `s[0] = 9` goes through to the caller's values. `s = []int{4}` only repoints the function's copy, so main still sees [9 2].

exercises.title: Send a piece
exercises.guide: Pass only a piece of a slice to a function.

chunks.guide: The function adds 1 to every value it receives.
A piece shares the values, so the original changes only there.

exercises.title: Return a slice
exercises.guide: Build a slice in a function and give it back.

chunks.guide: Make the slice, fill it by index and return it. No length in the result type.
The caller gets the slice the function made.
